claims.statement: AuthMiddleware is a plain ASGI middleware (not BaseHTTPMiddleware, to keep chat streaming) that resolves the caller once per request, skips non-HTTP scopes and the open paths /health, /docs, /docs/oauth2-redirect, /redoc and /openapi.json, answers bad tokens with its own JSON 401, and stores principal, db_role and db_claims in request state. It is added before CORSMiddleware so CORS wraps it.

resolve_principal depends on SUPABASE_URL and DEV_AUTH: with SUPABASE_URL unset every request is the seeded staff DEV_USER (except the local @local.test sign-in); with it set, no Authorization header is ANONYMOUS, 'Bearer dev' is DEV_USER only when DEV_AUTH is on (local only), and any other bearer token is verified as a Supabase access token; malformed or invalid headers are 401.

Supabase token verification fetches the project's JWKS through a cached PyJWKClient, accepts ES256 and RS256, requires audience 'authenticated', issuer <SUPABASE_URL>/auth/v1 and the exp, sub, aud and iss claims; the sub must be a UUID and the token must carry an email, otherwise 401.

A verified token is mapped to a users row on the owner pool by resolve_auth_user: look up by auth_user_id (syncing email), else link a staff-pre-created row with the same email and null auth_user_id, else insert; an email linked to a different Supabase account raises EmailTakenError, returned as 409. The sign-up trigger from migration 0022 normally creates the row first and downgrades its errors to warnings.

The dev user has no Supabase account; migration 0026 sets its users.auth_user_id to its own id and the backend sends that as the sub claim, so even in auth-off mode the dev user runs as the authenticated Postgres role under RLS (as staff) rather than bypassing it.

Route gates read the principal left by the middleware: require_user and require_principal return 401 when anonymous, require_staff adds a 403 for non-staff, require_scout returns 403 unless the caller is staff or a steward of some org, and chat_access requires sign-in and a new or owned thread, with someone else's thread returning 404 even for staff. The AGENT_ACCESS table in lifespan wires /agent to ask_access, /ingest to require_scout then chat_access, and /proposal to proposal_chat_access, and a path missing from it fails at boot.

CallerPool wraps the shared owner-connected psycopg pool: each connection() opens a transaction and calls set_caller, which sets the Postgres role (anon or authenticated) and request.jwt.claims with transaction-local set_config, so the connection returns to the pool as the owner and the checkpointer and agent tools never inherit a caller. get_caller_pool falls back to anon without middleware state, and PoolDep is what routers take.

The identity sent to Postgres is derived by _db_identity: anonymous gives role anon with empty claims, a signed-in caller gives role authenticated with claims containing the auth_user_id as sub, role and email.

The owner pool (OwnerPoolDep and get_pool()) bypasses grants and RLS and is used by identity code (resolve_principal, thread claiming, can_open_thread checks, request_scope), matching tools, all Import tools, the proposal agent's tools and context, Import's owner-side REST handlers, the matching run and the make match CLI, so those paths must check scope themselves.

CallerScope carries user_id, is_staff and org_id-to-role maps and implements the Python-side checks used by owner-pool code: can_read_org (staff or any role in the org), can_research_org (staff or steward of the org), can_save_funder, can_edit_proposal (staff, or admin or steward of the org, mirroring the 0048 RLS), and steward_of. It is built by caller_scope, skipping membership lookup for staff and anonymous callers.

Chat runs receive their CallerScope through the chat_scope ContextVar set by chat_access (and by proposal_chat_access, which also sets chat_proposal), and Import tools read it via ingest.caller.scope(); outside a chat request the scope is empty and non-staff, so gated tools refuse. staff_only returns a REFUSED message for non-staff and guards staff-only tools such as plan_import, run_import_now and read_workbook; without_private strips private findings for non-staff.

REST routes that read data Import keeps off RLS take the request_scope dependency, which builds a CallerScope on the owner pool for the signed-in caller, and filter in Python (for example list_research shows staff everything but others only what they saved plus NGOs they steward).

Migration 0023 creates the NOLOGIN NOINHERIT roles anon and authenticated when missing and ensures the connecting role can switch to them; the backend never connects as them but switches with set_config('role').

Migration 0024 defines SECURITY DEFINER access functions with a fixed search_path: app.user_id, app.is_staff, app.my_org_ids (any org role, so stewards read) and app.my_writable_org_ids (member and admin only), executable by anon and authenticated; app.can_open_thread takes the user as an argument and is granted to neither role because the owner-connected backend calls it.

Migration 0025 revokes all table and sequence privileges (and defaults) on public from anon and authenticated, grants back per table kind (public-readable, signed-in-only, closed), fails if a table has no access decision, and grants authenticated only specific writes (contacts, documents, score_adjustments, rfp_matches update, proposals, threads insert) with no DELETE.

Migration 0027 enables RLS on every public table and creates one read policy per table kind: public USING(true) tables, org and funder children that follow their parent, orgs and funders public unless hidden, contacts/documents/org_identifiers public by flag with org people and staff seeing more, chunks following documents, org-private proposals and rfp_matches, own-row users/org_members/threads, and staff-only Import tables; it fails the migration if a readable table lacks a read policy.

RLS write policies from 0027 let a member or admin of the row's org (never a steward) write contacts, score adjustments and rfp_matches updates, with staff also allowed, and threads insert only as oneself; 0048 replaced the proposal and document-insert rules.

Org membership is managed through SECURITY DEFINER functions (add_org_member, set_org_member_role, remove_org_member) that require app.can_manage_org (staff or admin of the org), keep at least one admin, and only add users who have signed in; a unique index allows an admin or member to belong to one org only, while stewards may support several, and the index holds even for the owner.

Funder Match runs are saved under RLS in migration 0042: app.my_match_org_ids covers admin and steward, funder_matches inserts require run_by to equal app.user_id and staff or a match org, and there is no update grant; matching.may_run mirrors the rule on the owner pool.
A table that the caller's Postgres role has no grant on raises InsufficientPrivilege, which create_app maps to a 403 with detail 'Not allowed' instead of a 500.

The Next.js proxy runs Supabase updateSession on all non-asset paths: without Supabase env keys it gates nothing; otherwise it refreshes the session via getClaims and redirects signed-out visitors on /import to /auth/login with a next parameter, while /ask stays public. Real enforcement is in the backend, which receives the Bearer access token.

Not yet built: auth plan Part 2 (full per-route and per-table test matrix, grant/revoke functions with audit log, management screens, re-linking recreated accounts, email-domain matching and join requests), and the plan itself is still marked draft.

Ask Sangam's SQL runs as the caller: ask_access claims the thread and stores the caller's (role, claims) in the agent_caller ContextVar, and PsycopgExecutor.run, inside one transaction, applies read-only and timeout hardening then set_caller with that identity, defaulting to anon when unset. The connection still comes from get_pool(), but RLS applies to the query; Import keeps the owner because it writes the catalog.

Since migration 0048, proposals_insert and proposals_update require the org to be in app.my_match_org_ids() (admin or steward) or the caller to be staff, so members still read proposals but can no longer write them; the same migration widens documents_insert to every role in the org (app.my_org_ids()) or staff, and re-runs the guard that every readable table has a read rule.

proposal_chat_access gates the /proposal chat: the thread id must be proposal-<id>-<caller's user id> (otherwise 404), the proposal's org must be readable to the caller (else 404, so strangers learn nothing), a reader who cannot edit (a member) gets 403, and only then is the thread claimed with use_case 'proposal' and chat_user_id, chat_scope and chat_proposal set. Each person therefore has a private chat per proposal.

Proposal write permission is enforced in three agreeing places: RLS on the caller pool (the proposals router uses PoolDep and computes can_edit in SQL from app.my_match_org_ids and app.is_staff, answering 403 for readers), proposal_chat_access for the chat route, and require_edit in the proposal agent's tools, which run on the owner pool and check scope.can_edit_proposal before any change.

Creating a proposal requires the caller to read the org and to have may_run on it (admin, steward or staff), otherwise 403; the proposal chat's saved-messages route reads the proposal on the caller pool and opens the caller's own thread through the owner pool.
The whole /ingest REST router and the /ingest chat route sit behind require_scout, built on request_scope, which allows only staff or a steward of at least one org and answers 403 otherwise.

When SUPABASE_URL is unset and DEV_AUTH is on, 'Bearer dev:<email>' signs in as a seeded @local.test user with an auth_user_id (other domains or unknown emails are 401), so roles can be tried locally without Supabase.

Frontend authHeaders (client) and serverAuthHeaders (server components) send Authorization: Bearer <Supabase session access token>, or nothing when signed out; when DEV_LOGIN is true (no NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_DEV_AUTH=1) they instead send Bearer dev:<email> from the sangam-dev-as cookie.
